title: Why Teaching Maths Will Always Be Chalk and Talk (but the Chalk Might Sprout Wings)
author: JFinB
summary: The piece argues that mathematics teaching is irreducibly a 'chalk and talk' act because maths can only be conveyed through a combination of language, visual representation, symbolism, and transformation over time -- no single medium suffices on its own. The author explains why isolating any one of these channels fails to convey mathematical meaning, and frames the teacher's live explanation as a 'pantomime act' that synchronizes these elements within students' limited attention spans. Rather than treating this as an argument against technology, the piece pivots to describe a tool the author built -- flipper.school -- that uses AI to match the best five-minute YouTube maths explainer videos to each small step of the White Rose curriculum, solving the problem that good teaching content exists online but is buried by an algorithm optimized for distraction rather than education. The article closes by reframing 'chalk' as an evolving medium: the delivery method is expanding to include curated video, but the fundamental need for synchronized, teacher-guided explanation remains constant.
points: Argues mathematical understanding requires the simultaneous combination of language, visual representation, symbolic notation, and stepwise transformation -- remove any one and comprehension collapses.
Frames live teacher explanation as a timing-dependent 'pantomime act' that must parse the target concept from competing distractions in real time, or risk losing the class.

Identifies a specific failure of ed-tech: enormous amounts of quality maths instruction already exist on YouTube, but the platform's discovery algorithm is optimized for engagement, not learning, so good content stays buried.

Describes flipper.school, a tool using LLM techniques to match transcript content (not just video titles) to White Rose curriculum small-steps, reducing the 'mis-cueing' problem of keyword-based search.
quotes: There has always and will always be a part of teaching maths that is chalk and talk, standing at the front illustrating ideas with visual imagery and symbols. Arguably, this is because of a fundamental law of communicating maths, mathematics can only be conveyed in a combination of language, visual representation, symbolism and transformations over time.

So we use chalk (or its modern equivalent) because it allows us the dynamism to draw, notate and make changes all whilst talking them through it. It's quite a pantomime act, an art, a skill, all to be done within the tiny attention spans of reluctant children.

But good ones are hard to find, YouTube is designed to distract you with all manner of shiny lures, it's not trying to help you educate yourself. You have to wrestle the algorithm to give up the good stuff.
It uses Large Language Model process techniques to match White Rise Small steps the actual words spoken in the transcripts of the videos. So no miscuing by video title.

Chalk and talk will always be the main medium via which maths is passed forward, however, the chalk is now available in a variety of other formats, fancy graphics, animations, new forms of concrete, pictorial and symbolic (CPA), why shouldn't teaching be supplemented by making use of them?
